newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka rate hike diversifies fund raising.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka rate hike diversifies fund raising.

text.p: Interest rate volatility in Sri Lanka has forced banks and companies to tighten treasury controls and diversify fund raising sources, treasury managers and analysts said on Thursday.
Banks and corporates which had made a habit of utilising short-term funds for long-term requirements took a kidney punch when short-term interest rates soared late last year.
"Up till then, banks were taking one day at a time cushioned by fat profit margins," said Mangala Boyagoda Treasury Manager of Union Bank of Colombo.
"But high rates forced banks to adopt scientific treasury management and take steps to hedge positive and negative gaps," he said.

A flurry of new savings schemes have been launched by banks so far this year while a growing number of companies rushed to cut exposure to short-term debt through debentures, floating rate notes and certificates of deposit and securitisations.

The average call money rate in the last quarter of 1995 skyrocketed to 30.9 percent, against an overall 1995 average of about 20, after the government's defence spending exceeded budget by 10 billion rupees ($178.6 million) following an end to a truce in its war with separatist Tamil rebels.
The problem was compounded by two development banks which resorted to short-term funds due to delays in sourcing longer term credit lines, dealers said.

"Necessity was the mother of invention. If not for the rate volatility no one would have thought twice about carrying a huge gap between assets and liabilities," said Freddie Jayarajah, Deputy General Manager of the state-owned Bank of Ceylon.

The positive impact of tight treasury management has pushed down money market rates, despite the government's continued heavy defence expenditure which is expected to again overshoot budget by 10 billion rupees this year, dealers said.
"The average money rate from January to August 1996 was 13.8 percent. I doubt the yearly average being beyond 15 percent," said Shantha Balasuriya, senior interbank dealer at Standard Chartered Bank.
The Bank of Ceylon sold four-year debentures for 5.5 billion rupees, raised $12 million with three-year floating rate certificates of deposit and launched a family savings scheme this year.
Hatton National Bank Ltd has launched medium-term floating rate notes, and introduced a seven-year savings scheme. Commercial Bank Ltd and Seylan Bank Ltd have also launched savings schemes.
The main corporates that securitised debt are Lanka Orix Leasing Ltd and Vanik Inc Ltd

Lanka Orix secured 300 million rupees through four-year promissory notes last month after securitising lease receivables for 400 million rupees last November which cut company's short-term debt to 50 percent from 60 percent.
Vanik in April raised 150 million rupees with an unsecured convertible debenture at 20 percent, which is now trading publicly in Colombo.

"1996 earnings per share forecasts for the banking sector are 2.1 percent, down from 16.6 percent in 1995... the impact of high interest rates in late 1995 will be felt only in 1996," said Panduka Ambanpola of brokerage Jardine Fleming.
Jardine Fleming's 1997 EPS growth forecast for the banking sector is 13.4 percent, he said.
